Intrinsic motivation results in students who have a genuine interest in the subject matter and learn for the sake of learning. They enjoy exploring and mastering the material. They don't see learning as a means to an end. Instead, learning math concepts or classic literature provides them with emotional and intellectual satisfaction. Intrinsic motivation has long-term consequences, frequently propelling people to be lifelong learners and even leading them to careers they will enjoy in the future.Intrinsic motivation takes time to develop, which can be difficult in a world that demands instant gratification. To encourage this type of learning, you must work hard as your child grows. Furthermore, some students simply do not respond to this approach. Extrinsic motivation may be more effective for an individual student's learning style in some cases.

Bruner (1962) has been suggested the most important ways to help students think and learn is to free them from the control of rewards and punishments. By learning what to do to get rewards and by doing just what the teacher wants, students can become overachievers, but will fail to develop the capacity to transform their learning into flexible, useful cognitive structures.
